hub.title: Your first pull request starts here
hub.lede: Beginner-friendly issues from open-source projects with Algerian maintainers or a clear link to Algeria. Every listed project pledges to answer newcomers within 7 days.
hub.no_match: Try another language or label, or clear the filters.
hub.note: Open issues labelled {gfi} or {hw} in listed projects, refreshed from GitHub every {hours} hours. Each card links to the issue on GitHub.
hub.empty_title: The first projects are being listed.
hub.empty: Their beginner issues appear here as soon as they pass the seven listing checks. Maintain an open-source project with a link to Algeria? Listing it takes one pull request, and no account.
hub.step1: Comment on it to say you’re working on it, so nobody duplicates your work.
hub.step2_t: Open a draft pull request early
hub.step2: Push a first version and ask questions in the pull request. Small is fine.
hub.step3: Listed maintainers pledge to review or answer newcomers within a week.
hub.ideas_lede: Anyone can propose an open-source project that would help people in Algeria, and anyone with a GitHub account can vote. Every quarter, djazair.dev adopts the idea with the most votes and builds it in the open.
hub.idea1: Say what is hard or missing, who it would help and the skills it needs, in English or Arabic. The form on GitHub asks for each, and for a champion to lead it.
hub.idea2: Anyone with a GitHub account can upvote an idea, once. Votes carry over from one quarter to the next until the idea is adopted.
hub.idea3: When a quarter ends, the maintainers review the ideas with the most votes. The first with at least {votes} and a champion is adopted: it gets a repository in djazair.dev’s GitHub organisation and a place in the Hub.
hub.ideas_closes: Voting closes at the end of {date}, UTC.
hub.ideas_empty: Propose the first one: voting starts as soon as it’s posted.
hub.ideas_note: Votes are GitHub upvotes, one per account, and this list is refreshed every {hours} hours. When a round closes, the next Hub sync saves its count on GitHub: see {results}.
hub.numbers_title: New contributors, and how fast they hear back
hub.numbers_lede: Counted each day from the pull requests and issues of the projects the Hub shows. A new contributor is someone whose first pull request to one of them was merged that quarter, bots and maintainers aside. A response is a maintainer’s first comment or review, or the merge. Only these counts are kept, never usernames.
hub.numbers_caption: New contributors and first responses, by quarter
hub.numbers_note: Counted on {date} for the {n} projects the Hub showed that day. When a project joins or leaves, past quarters change with it.
hub.translate_lede: Volunteer teams translate Firefox, LibreOffice, Mastodon and other open-source software into Arabic and Tamazight. You can join one with a browser and a free account.
hub.projects_lede: Every listed project passes a daily health check: recent commits, open beginner issues and the djazairdev topic. Dashed cards are projects Algeria’s ecosystem still needs.
hub.projects_note: A project that fails a check for 14 days is hidden until it’s fixed, and one that removes the topic leaves at once. {report}.

hub.list_lede: Add one entry to projects.yml, or fill in the issue form if you’d rather not use git. No djazair.dev account needed: the djazairdev topic proves you maintain the repository.

check.docs: A README and a CONTRIBUTING file
check.issues: At least 3 open issues labelled {gfi} or {hw}
check.pledge: Maintainers pledge to reply to newcomer pull requests within 7 days
check.topic: The repository carries the GitHub topic {topic}
check.relevance: Algerian maintainers, or clear relevance to Algeria

hub.check_note: A failing check names what to fix. A code of conduct is recommended, not required.
hub.list_note: Submissions are reviewed in public within 7 days. Language, licence and activity are read from GitHub, so the entry stays short.

localisation.title: Translate software into Arabic and Tamazight
localisation.lede: Volunteer teams translate Firefox, LibreOffice, Mastodon and other open-source software on Pontoon, Weblate and Crowdin. No code needed: a browser, a free account and a good command of the language are enough.
localisation.arabic_lede: Most of these projects are partly translated into Arabic. Every release brings new strings, and suggestions wait for a reviewer before they reach users.
localisation.tamazight_lede: Kabyle (Taqbaylit), written in Latin script, has teams on all three platforms. Tamazight in Tifinagh has smaller teams that follow the standard used in Morocco. Chaouia, Mozabite and Tamahaq don’t have their own language on these platforms yet: a new team starts by asking the platform to add one.
localisation.step1: Your translation reaches everyone who uses it in your language. Each link above opens the team’s page.
localisation.step2_t: Sign up and read the guide
localisation.step2: Create a free account on the platform. If the team has a style guide or a glossary, read it first: it keeps each term translated the same way everywhere.
localisation.step3: New translators usually make suggestions that an experienced member approves. Once you know the terms, offer to review: it is where many teams fall behind.
localisation.rules: The list lives in {file}. Add a team with a pull request, or open an issue with its link. It should be a public team on Pontoon, Weblate or Crowdin that translates open-source software into Arabic or Tamazight and welcomes new translators.
localisation.checked: Every link was checked on {date}, and a weekly check reports any that break.
localisation.index_t: This work doesn’t show up in the Index
localisation.index: Pontoon, Weblate and Crowdin commit translations to the projects’ repositories from their own servers, and GitHub places each push where it comes from. So translation work counts where the servers are, not in Algeria. The Index can’t see it, but everyone using the software in Arabic or Tamazight can. See the {limits}.

meetups.title: Meet over coffee
meetups.lede: Small, free meetups in cafés in Algerian cities, for founders, builders and the developers who work with them. No invitation, title or pitch deck needed. They are organised on {platform}, djazair.dev’s sister project.
meetups.what_title: A small table and a subject
meetups.what1: A small group meets in a real café to talk about the subject the host described.
meetups.what2: Talk about your work and what you’re stuck on. Don’t use the meetup to promote a product or service.
meetups.what3: There’s no fee to join or to host. Everyone pays for their own order.
meetups.host_title: No meetup in your city yet? Host the first one
meetups.host_lede: Anyone can host. Whoever publishes a meetup runs it.
meetups.step1_t: Pick a café and a time
meetups.step1: Somewhere easy to reach, with room for a small group.
meetups.step2: One subject, so people know what they’re coming to talk about.
meetups.step3: People confirm on the meetup’s page. On the day, the host posts the table number there.
meetups.bring_title: Something to bring to the table
meetups.bring_hub: Pick a beginner-friendly issue from the Project Hub and work on it together.
meetups.bring_report: Talk through what the quarterly report says about Algeria’s developers.
meetups.note: It has its own accounts, {terms} and {privacy}. djazair.dev has no accounts and shares nothing with it: these are plain links.

definitions.accounts: All GitHub accounts located in Algeria, including inactive accounts.
definitions.pushes: Git pushes during the quarter, divided by all accounts. One push can contain several commits.
definitions.repos: Public repositories divided by all accounts. Both are running totals.
definitions.orgs: GitHub organisations divided by all accounts. These can be teams, companies or clubs.
definitions.topics: Topics GitHub reports when at least 100 developers in Algeria use them. Smaller topics are hidden.
definitions.permillion: GitHub accounts for every 1 million residents. Adjusts community size for population.

languages.rw_markup_text: GitHub detects languages from the files pushed, so markup such as HTML and CSS, Jupyter notebooks and files such as Dockerfile count too.

collaboration.lede_down: In {quarter}, repositories owned in {first} received the most pushes and pull requests from developers in Algeria: {a}, down from {before} a year earlier.
collaboration.lede_same: In {quarter}, repositories owned in {first} received the most pushes and pull requests from developers in Algeria: {a}, the same as a year earlier.

collaboration.eu_other: GitHub also lists the European Union, at {eu}. It overlaps with its members above, so the bars leave it out.

collaboration.fig2_summary: Git pushes and pull requests that developers in each listed economy sent to repositories owned in Algeria in {quarter}, and the change from a year earlier.

collaboration.fig3_summary: Every quarter since {from}: the pushes and pull requests developers in Algeria sent to repositories owned in the listed economies, and those repositories owned in Algeria received from them. In {last}, {sent} sent and {received} received.
collaboration.fig3_source: Source: GitHub Innovation Graph (CC0), {from} to {to}. Sums over the economies GitHub lists each quarter, without the European Union.
collaboration.lede3: In {first}, developers in Algeria sent {s0} pushes and pull requests to repositories owned in the economies listed, and repositories owned in Algeria received {r0}. In {last}: {s1} sent and {r1} received.
collaboration.both_lede: Every economy GitHub lists with Algeria in {quarter}, in either direction. A dash means GitHub didn’t list the pair that way: it was below the threshold.
collaboration.both_caption: Pushes and pull requests between Algeria and each listed economy, {quarter}

collaboration.rw_owner_text: A repository counts in its owner’s economy, and an organisation’s repositories where most of its members are. A project with contributors in many economies counts toward one, so GitHub calls this a lower bound.
collaboration.rw_threshold_text: GitHub lists a pair of economies only above its publication threshold. Smaller partners are missing, and an economy can appear one quarter and not the next.
collaboration.rw_eu_text: GitHub lists the EU as one economy as well. Its figure is the sum of the members listed, so this page leaves it out of rankings and totals. The downloads keep it.
collaboration.rw_place_text: Developers are placed by their network address. A VPN moves a developer’s work to another economy, which can add or hide partners.

rankings.title: GitHub’s Africa ranking, GDC26
rankings.lede: For the Global Digital Collaboration Conference in Geneva, 1–3 September 2026, GitHub ranked economies by git pushes per 1,000 working-age people, corrected for VPN use. It is a one-off dataset, outside the quarterly Index. Algeria isn’t in Africa’s top ten, so its figure here is djazair.dev’s estimate.

rankings.check_unlisted: Core peers GitHub doesn’t list, by the same estimate: {list}.
rankings.check_caption: GitHub’s GDC26 figures against djazair.dev’s estimate
rankings.check_source: Source: GitHub, GDC26 supplementary data (CC0); djazair.dev’s estimate from the GitHub Innovation Graph and the World Bank.
rankings.rw_once_text: GitHub prepared these lists once, for GDC26. They aren’t part of the quarterly Index and won’t change when new data comes out.
rankings.rw_vpn_text: GitHub moved pushes between economies by comparing the locations in developers’ profiles with where their network addresses place them. Nobody outside GitHub can repeat the correction.
rankings.rw_estimate_text: Algeria’s figure here uses network addresses only, and repeats the latest quarter for any not released yet. It shows roughly where Algeria stands, not a place GitHub gave it.
rankings.rw_people_text: The lists divide by people aged 15 to 64, not by all people or by developers. GitHub left out economies under 200,000 people.

methodology.lede: Every number on djazair.dev comes from public data and published code. This page lists the sources, formulas, peer groups and known limits, so anyone can check a figure or reproduce it.

about.title: About djazair.dev
about.lede: An open scorecard of Algeria’s developer ecosystem and a hub for its open-source projects, built in the open.
about.analytics_on: We count visits with Cloudflare Web Analytics, which uses no cookies and doesn’t follow you from site to site: it keeps totals only, such as pages viewed, countries and browsers.
about.hub_ideas: It also shows project ideas from GitHub Discussions with their number of votes, never who proposed or voted for them.
about.hub_counts: It also counts new contributors and response times from the listed projects’ public pull requests and issues: usernames are read during the count and never kept.

downloads.title: Data and downloads
downloads.lede: Every table behind the Index as CSV and JSON, free to reuse under CC0. Each quarter’s files stay online with a manifest of checksums, and every change is logged.
downloads.tables_lede: The {n} tables of the {quarter} data, computed from GitHub Innovation Graph release {release}. The data dictionary describes every column.
downloads.checksums: The manifest lists every file with its size and SHA-256 checksum, so you can check what you downloaded.
downloads.earlier_none: {quarter} is the first quarter published. Earlier quarters will stay online, unchanged, as new ones arrive.
downloads.charts_lede: The figures behind every chart on the site, as CSV and JSON. Each chart’s download menu also has SVG and PNG files, dark or light.
downloads.addresses_lede: Stable addresses, served with CORS, so code and pages on other sites can fetch them. latest.json names the newest quarter’s folder; a folder never changes once a newer quarter is out.
downloads.changelog_lede: One entry per data release, with any revised past values flagged, and the changes to the site worth knowing about.
downloads.corrections_lede: Every correction to a published number or statement, with the date the error was found and the date it was fixed. Corrections are published within 7 days of discovery.
downloads.licence_lede: The derived data is CC0 1.0: use it for anything, without asking. Credit is welcome, not required. Accounts per million people also uses World Bank population, which is CC BY 4.0: when you reuse that column, credit the World Bank. Text and charts on the site are CC BY 4.0.
downloads.attribution_text: Data: GitHub Innovation Graph (CC0) · djazair.dev. Population: World Bank (CC BY 4.0).

rule.accounts_text: The data counts accounts, dormant ones included, so headlines say “developer accounts”.
rule.bad_news: Bad news as clearly as good
rule.bad_news_text: A fall gets the same space and the same plain words as a rise.
rule.medians_text: Algeria is compared with the median of each peer group rather than with one neighbour.
rule.checked_text: Before a report is published, someone other than its author checks every number against the published data, and a fluent reader checks each translation.
rule.corrections_text: Mistakes are fixed and listed in the corrections log within 7 days of being found. We never credit GitHub with a claim it didn’t make.
